paras: The Macon, Mississippi floggings of 1919 were an attack on Saturday night, June 7, 1919, in which white men flogged several leading Black citizens of Macon and white residents then robbed Black homes and stores. No arrests had been reported by mid-June. The New York Age editorialized on the case because, by its account, a banker, a deputy sheriff and the city marshal led the floggings.

The men attacked were Black property owners of means, among them Mr. Young, said to run one of the town's best stores. According to the New York Age, the assailants accused their victims of having advised Negroes to demand better pay for their work, and one man was punished for saying "Yes" and "No" to a white man. The Chicago Defender instead attributed Young's beating to white resentment of his prosperity.

The Defender wrote that white citizens had "carefully perfected plans" and struck suddenly that night. A Prof. Hicks was whipped on his bare back, James Little was flogged and his house robbed of $150, and Young was beaten and his store wrecked; other men were also whipped. Encouraged by the officials' example, a white "rabble" then pillaged Black-owned houses and stores and intimidated their owners. The victims were ordered to leave town so that others might take their property, and at least one man was led out of town after the whipping.
The New York Age reported that no arrests had been made; no report of a prosecution appears in the coverage.

Only the Black press carried the story, on June 21, 1919. The New York Age ran a news item headlined "Flogged by the 'Better Element' in Mississippi" and an editorial, "The Better Element," which argued that the case was a "severe setback" to the idea that mob violence came from "the ignorant class of poor whites" against the judgment of the educated. The Chicago Defender placed its account on page one under the subheads "Cause of Flogging" and "Plans Well Formed," and framed the attack as a scheme by whites "to gain their valuable holdings."

bases: A band of white men, including local officials, flogged prosperous Black property owners and ordered them to leave town so that others might take their property, while others robbed Black homes and stores (A2, A3, A4).

The Chicago Defender (A2) and the New York Age (A3, A4) both report the June 7 floggings of Black property owners, both name Mr. Young, and their differing details (Hicks named only in A2, Little only in A4) suggest separate sources.

accounts.label: New York Age correspondent ('authentic information')
accounts.gist: A banker, a deputy sheriff and the city marshal flogged leading Black citizens for advising Negroes to demand better pay; white ruffians then robbed Black homes, and the victims were ordered to leave so others could get their property.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender correspondent
accounts.gist: White citizens planned the floggings for Saturday night, June 7, struck suddenly, pillaged homes, and aimed to gain the victims' valuable holdings; Young was beaten because of his prosperity.

framing.detail: The New York Age headlined the news 'Flogged by the "Better Element" in Mississippi' and editorialized under 'The Better Element' that the case set back the claim that mob violence came only from poor whites.
The Chicago Defender ran it on page one under the subheads 'Cause of Flogging' and 'Plans Well Formed', presenting the attack as a planned scheme to seize Black property.
